concepts.def: Adapting what you say and how you say it to suit the listeners, their age, knowledge and expectations in a given speaking situation.
The level of formality of language chosen to suit a context, from formal Standard English in a presentation to informal speech among friends.
Body language, eye contact, gesture and facial expression that support a spoken message and help to engage and persuade listeners.
Paying close attention to a speaker, responding appropriately, asking questions and showing understanding rather than simply waiting to talk.
The widely accepted form of English, with conventional grammar and vocabulary, often expected in formal spoken presentations.
The orderly exchange of speaking roles in a discussion, allowing participants to contribute, respond and build on each other's points.

walkthroughs.body_html:
Unit 2: Speaking and Listening — a core area of GCSE English Language.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Unit 2: Speaking and Listening brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Unit 2: Speaking and Listening.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: Adjusting your vocabulary and tone to suit your listeners is known as:
options: Audience awareness
Proofreading
Skimming
Drafting

mcqs.q: Eye contact, gesture and facial expression are forms of:
options: Non-verbal communication
Standard spelling
Punctuation
Paragraphing

mcqs.q: In a formal presentation to an examiner, the most appropriate register is:
options: Formal Standard English
Slang and abbreviations
Text-message language
Total silence

mcqs.q: Listening attentively and responding to what others say in a discussion is called:
options: Active listening
Skimming
Scanning
Drafting

mcqs.q: Are spoken fillers such as 'um' and 'you know' always a sign of poor speaking?
options: Speaking well depends only on how loudly you talk.
They always mean the speaker is unprepared and a poor communicator.
They are spelling mistakes.
No; they are a natural feature of spontaneous speech and can give thinking time, though too many can distract.

mcqs.q: Is formal Standard English always the best choice when speaking?
options: You should never use Standard English when speaking.
No; the right register depends on audience and purpose, so informal speech may suit a casual context.
They are spelling mistakes.
Formal Standard English is correct in every speaking situation.

mcqs.q: Does good speaking depend only on the words you say?
options: Speaking well depends only on how loudly you talk.
They are spelling mistakes.
Only the words matter; body language is irrelevant.
No; non-verbal communication such as eye contact, tone and gesture is also vital to delivery.
